lesson.title: Resistance Gets a Phase Angle: Introducing Impedance
lesson.summary: Impedance Z = R + jX packages a circuit element's opposition to AC current, both how much it resists and how much it shifts the phase between voltage and current, into a single complex number.
lesson.body:
In a purely resistive DC circuit, Ohm's law V = IR is the whole story: current and voltage rise and fall together, and R alone tells you how much current a given voltage produces. Add an inductor or a capacitor to an AC circuit, though, and Ohm's law in that simple form breaks down. Reactance, the opposition an inductor or capacitor offers to a changing current, does not dissipate energy the way resistance does; instead it shifts the timing between voltage and current by up to 90 degrees. Because resistance and reactance affect a signal in fundamentally different ways, in phase versus in quadrature, we cannot just add their ohm values together as ordinary numbers. Instead we combine them as a complex impedance Z = R + jX, where R is the real part and X is the imaginary part, both measured in ohms.

Writing Z as a complex number lets us describe both magnitude and phase in one symbol. Its magnitude, |Z| = sqrt(R^2 + X^2), tells you how much the impedance restricts the RMS current for a given RMS voltage, exactly like a resistance would in DC. Its angle, theta = arctan(X / R), tells you the phase difference between voltage and current: a positive X (inductive) means voltage leads current, a negative X (capacitive) means current leads voltage. With impedance defined this way, Ohm's law survives intact in phasor form: V = I Z, where V and I are now phasors, complex numbers representing amplitude and phase, rather than plain real numbers.

It helps to picture Z as a point in the complex plane, R measured along the horizontal axis and X along the vertical axis. That geometric picture is exactly complex impedance: the same quantity expressed either in rectangular form (R, X) or in polar form (|Z|, theta), with straightforward trigonometry converting between them. Addition of impedances in series works cleanly in rectangular form, since you just add the real parts and add the imaginary parts, which is one more reason engineers keep both representations on hand.

Take a series RL circuit with R = 30 ohms and inductive reactance XL = 40 ohms, driven by a 100 V RMS sinusoidal source. The impedance is Z = 30 + j40 ohms. Its magnitude is |Z| = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = sqrt(900 + 1600) = sqrt(2500) = 50 ohms, and its angle is theta = arctan(40/30) = arctan(1.333) = 53.13 degrees. The RMS current is I = V/Z = 100 V / 50 ohms = 2 A, and because theta is positive, that current lags the voltage by 53.13 degrees. Notice that the 50 ohm magnitude, not 30 or 40 alone, is what actually limits the current, exactly as plain resistance would in a DC circuit.

Impedance is the hub that the rest of AC circuit theory hangs from. Take its reciprocal and you get admittance, which is more convenient for parallel circuits. Split it into a right triangle of R and X and you get the impedance triangle, a visual tool for the same relationship derived here. And once every element in a circuit is expressed as an impedance, Kirchhoff's laws and all the DC circuit techniques you already know apply again, just with complex numbers standing in for real ones.
